name: Shrimp Welfare Project (charityevals)
summary: Shrimp Welfare Project buys electrical stunners and gives them to large shrimp producers in Asia and Latin America (its Humane Slaughter Initiative), on condition that they stun at least about 1,900 tonnes of shrimp a year, so the shrimp are unconscious before they go into ice slurry. Using its audited UK accounts for April 2024 to March 2025 and the stunners it bought that year, we estimate about 15 suffering-adjusted days (SADs) averted per dollar you give, about 3.9 times GiveDirectly at the default exchange rates. The result is mostly uncertainty: how long a shrimp suffers when chilled alive, how intense that pain is and how much it counts moves it from about 0.35 to 70 times GiveDirectly on its own (0.013 to 620 times with all of our inputs at their ends and the shared exchange rates at their defaults). We use Ambitious Impact's 2024 SAD method, which the site's other SAD figures share, with Rethink Priorities' roughly 4 minutes of pain; Ambitious Impact's newer 2026 method would put SWP at about 0.6 times GiveDirectly, Rethink Priorities' pain weights at about 35 times, and Ambitious Impact's 2024 figure with 20 minutes of pain at about 67 times. The program's bet that early adopters tip the whole industry towards stunning is not counted.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the stunner program cost in Shrimp Welfare Project's financial year April 2024 to March 2025, including its share of overhead, from the audited accounts of the UK charity (the only legal entity SWP names). Costs are counted in cash: the stunners bought in the year are counted when bought, and the accounting depreciation on earlier stunners is taken out so nothing is counted twice.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: Shrimp per year that will be stunned by the stunners SWP bought in the year: stunners bought × tonnes each stunner handles a year × shrimp per tonne.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: Suffering spared for each shrimp that is stunned instead of dying conscious in ice slurry, and how many years earlier those producers stun than they would have without SWP.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for stunners that don't knock shrimp out reliably in commercial use, producers that would have stunned anyway, credit shared with retailers and producers, and stunners that are not installed or not used on the committed volume. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: Suffering-adjusted days (SADs) averted, in total and per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff and contractors who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With salary sacrifice counted, your dollar is credited with its share only.

rows.label: Pounds per US dollar, April 2024 to March 2025 average

source.title: IRS, Yearly average currency exchange rates

rows.explainer: SWP's financial year runs April 2024 to March 2025, nine months of which fall in 2024 (IRS average 0.783 £/$). The pound was weaker in January–March 2025 than over calendar 2025 as a whole (0.759), so the year's average is close to the 2024 rate; best 0.783. The range runs from the 2025 rate to 0.80 for a weaker-pound quarter. The effect on the result is under 2%.

rows.label: Total expenditure in the accounts (£)

source.title: Shrimp Welfare Project Ltd, audited accounts year ended 31 March 2025, Statement of Financial Activities

rows.explainer: Everything the charity spent in the year in its accounts, including £116,346 of depreciation on stunners bought earlier and a £64,373 foreign-exchange loss. The UK charity is the only entity SWP names on its website and team page; no US 990 or fiscal sponsor turned up, so we treat these accounts as the whole organisation. If some costs run through another entity, the cost here is too low. Two signs the accounts may not show SWP's full running cost: people costs (£375,000 of contractors and payroll) look small for a team with field coordinators in several countries, and the CEO's service fees fell from £61,278 to £16,162 (note 7). In addition, SWP raised £2.18 million and spent £593,000, ending the year with £2.65 million in cash, about four years of spending against a six-month reserves policy (p. 3). A new donation therefore mostly funds future years, when the budget is larger; this model uses the cost per shrimp of the year we have accounts for.

rows.label: Direct charitable-activity costs before support and governance costs (£)

source.title: Shrimp Welfare Project Ltd, audited accounts year ended 31 March 2025, note 5
source.page: p. 15, note 5 Analysis of expenditure, Charitable activities column

rows.explainer: Spending on all programs (stunners, the Sustainable Shrimp Farming in India program, corporate work on eyestalk ablation, research), before the £54,058 of support costs and £6,000 of governance costs are added. Includes the depreciation and the foreign-exchange loss.

rows.label: Depreciation on stunners already owned (£)

source.title: Shrimp Welfare Project Ltd, audited accounts year ended 31 March 2025, notes 5 and 9
source.page: p. 16, note 9 Tangible fixed assets, Depreciation charge for the year

rows.explainer: SWP keeps ownership of the stunners it gives producers, so they sit on its balance sheet as plant and machinery and are written down by 25% a year on a reducing balance. Depreciation is an accounting charge for stunners bought earlier, not cash spent this year; it is removed here and the year's stunner purchases are added instead, so each stunner is costed once, in the year it is bought.

rows.label: Stunners bought in the year (£)

source.title: Shrimp Welfare Project Ltd, audited accounts year ended 31 March 2025, note 9
source.page: p. 16, note 9 Tangible fixed assets (Plant and Machinery)

rows.explainer: Plant and machinery bought in the year. SWP's only capitalised equipment is the stunners it lends to producers (cost £241,959 at the start of the year, £630,121 at the end; none before April 2023), so we read the additions as stunner purchases. Producers pay freight and import duties themselves.

rows.label: Total cash spending, all programs and overhead
rows.explainer: Total expenditure, minus depreciation, plus the stunners bought in the year, converted to dollars: about £865,000 or $1.11 million.

rows.label: Program cash spending, all programs
rows.explainer: Direct program spending on the same cash basis: about £805,000 or $1.04 million.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads support and governance costs (about 7% on top) over programs in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do.

rows.label: Stunner program's share of program costs other than stunners
rows.explainer: The accounts don't split costs by program. Besides buying stunners, the stunner program needs staff and contractors to find producers, negotiate agreements, install the equipment and train operators. SWP's other work in the year: the Sustainable Shrimp Farming in India program, corporate and retailer policies (for example Morrisons' shrimp welfare policy, eyestalk-ablation commitments), research such as the shrimp paste scoping report and the Welfare Index, and communications. Anchors: SWP's own 2025 '2030 vision' post (forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/Ztqzt4BWMPZW5ECfP) presents the Humane Slaughter Initiative and the India farm program as its two main programs, with the stunner program the larger by shrimp reached; the trustees' report for the year leads with corporate engagement and doesn't mention stunners. Best guess half of the non-stunner program costs (about £416,000 after taking out depreciation); low 30% if India, corporate and research work took most staff time, high 70% if most field staff worked on stunner deals and installation. A staff-time split from SWP would settle it.

rows.label: Spending on the stunner program (Humane Slaughter Initiative) in the year
rows.explainer: The stunners bought in the year plus the program's share of staff, contractor and other program costs, in dollars: about $760,000 at the best guess, of which about $500,000 is the stunners themselves.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled program, including overhead
Price of one stunner

source.title: Boddy & Jiménez Zorrilla (25 September 2023), Two years of Shrimp Welfare Project: insights and impact (EA Forum, SWP co-founders)
source.page: main post, Humane Slaughter Initiative section

rows.explainer: SWP's own figure from September 2023, the most recent published price. Its producers use two models (Ace Aquatec and Optimar) whose prices may differ, and three years of inflation and exchange-rate moves may have raised it, so the range is $55,000–80,000. It is consistent with the accounts: £241,959 of stunners by March 2024 (about $310,000, four to five stunners) and £630,121 (about $800,000, about 12 stunners) by March 2025.

rows.label: Stunners bought in the year
rows.explainer: The year's stunner purchases divided by the price of one stunner: about 7.6 at the best guess. SWP's public count of agreements went from four signed commitments in its September 2023 post (Two years of Shrimp Welfare Project) to 17 stunners agreed in its 2025 '2030 vision' post, and 37 by autumn 2026 (the (Shr)Impact page), so agreements ran ahead of purchases; agreements without a purchased stunner are not counted here.

rows.label: Shrimp stunned per stunner per year (tonnes)

source.title: Shrimp Welfare Project, (Shr)Impact page; Humane Slaughter Initiative page
source.quote: 20 stunners have been installed and commissioned, with an expected impact of 54,175 MT

rows.explainer: How much shrimp each stunner handles a year. SWP reports 54,175 tonnes a year for 20 installed stunners (2,709 each) and 89,774 tonnes for 37 signed agreements (2,426 each); best guess 2,550 sits between them. Low end: the contract minimum, 'at least 1,900 metric tonnes of shrimp annually' (Humane Slaughter Initiative page). High end: a little above the installed average. These are volumes producers commit to, not measured throughput; whether the stunner is actually used on all of it is in the delivery adjustment.

rows.label: Shrimp per tonne
rows.explainer: SWP converts tonnes to individuals with an average size: 3.6 billion shrimp for 54,175 tonnes is about 66,000 per tonne (15 g each), typical of whiteleg shrimp at harvest. Its range for all agreements, 4.5–9.0 billion for 89,774 tonnes, gives 50,000–100,000 per tonne (10–20 g), which we use as low and high. Larger tiger shrimp (30–40 g) would sit below the range.

rows.label: Shrimp per year stunned by the stunners bought in the year
rows.explainer: About 1.3 billion shrimp a year at the best guess. As a check, SWP's own public figure of about 1,400 shrimp helped per dollar per year implies a similar cost per shrimp to ours before any adjustment (1.3 billion ÷ $0.8 million is about 1,600). The template's 'share not yet compliant' step is left out because SWP's partners were not stunning before; producers that would have adopted stunning anyway are handled in counterfactual_adj.

rows.label: SADs averted per shrimp stunned instead of killed in ice slurry
rows.explainer: Each shrimp is slaughtered once, so a stunner's yearly throughput is the number of animals helped per year, and the benefit per animal is the slaughter pain it avoids. The shared fact applies Ambitious Impact's 2024 (v1) SAD method for shrimp stunning, the version behind the site's other SAD facts, to Rethink Priorities' estimate of how long ice-slurry slaughter hurts (about 48 seconds excruciating and 3 minutes disabling): 0.0056 SADs per shrimp, range 0.0005–0.1. Three readings bracket it: AIM's 2026 method (v2) gives about 0.0008 (about 0.6 times GiveDirectly); Rethink Priorities' mean pain weights give about 0.051 (about 35 times); AIM's v1 figure with its 20-minute duration, used by the site's Aquatic Life Institute model, gives 0.097 (about 67 times). See facts/sad_factors.json. This fact is the main uncertainty in the model.

rows.label: Years the stunning is brought forward
rows.explainer: How many years earlier these producers stun than they would have without SWP's stunner. Two limits apply. Equipment life: SWP grants producers 'indefinite usage' of the stunner while keeping ownership (Humane Slaughter Initiative page), so use is limited by the equipment, not the contract; SWP's accounts write the stunners down at 25% a year on a reducing balance, which implies no fixed life; industrial processing equipment of this kind is often kept longer, and a producer that has built stunning into its harvest and sales may keep doing it after the unit wears out, but we found no published service life. Counterfactual adoption: nothing obliges producers in Vietnam, India, Ecuador or Honduras to stun shrimp, and electrical stunning was close to absent before SWP's program; but UK and EU retailers (Tesco, M&S, Sainsbury's, Albert Heijn and others) now have public electrical-stunning commitments, so producers exporting to them might have adopted it within some years anyway. Best guess 5 years, a judgment: a few years of equipment life plus some continued use, short of the decade a well-kept unit might last. Low 2 years if retailer policies would soon have forced stunning anyway or units fail early; high 10 years for a long-lived unit at a producer selling to markets with no such pressure, or one that keeps stunning after the unit is replaced.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
rows.explainer: Years of impact discounted at the shared rate. The roughly six-month lead time from order to delivery is not discounted separately.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: stunning works as intended in commercial use
rows.explainer: The SAD figure already allows for 3% of shrimp missed by the stunner (AIM's 0.97, from a manufacturer case study) and otherwise assumes stunned shrimp are unconscious from the first second and stay so through the ice slurry; this adjustment covers worse performance in the field. The evidence that this happens is thin. The one controlled study on whiteleg shrimp (Somerville et al. 2026, University of Stirling, with EEG) found neural insensibility faster after electrical stunning than cold shock alone, but some stunned shrimp tail-flipped again in the ice slurry, mostly after the shorter, lower-voltage stun (2–2.5 V/cm for 5 s against 2.5–3 V/cm for 20 s), and insensibility was confirmed only in animals that did not respond to the cold shock. In commercial use, settings, water conductivity, batch size and operator practice vary, and nobody has published field checks of stun quality at SWP's partners. Best guess 0.7: most shrimp are stunned well, a minority get a partial stun and a share of the benefit. Low 0.4 if poor settings are common (an inadequate stun may be no better than ice slurry); high 0.9 if field stun quality matches the lab's stronger regime. Shrimp sentience is not discounted here: it is inside the welfare range in the SAD figure.

rows.label: Share of stunners producers would not have bought themselves at the time
rows.explainer: Some producers that took a free stunner might have bought one themselves around the same time, for example to meet a UK or EU buyer's stunning requirement; for them the credit is zero. For the others, how much earlier they stun is in years_of_impact, not here, so the two don't double count. Best guess 85%: the stunners cost about $65,000, SWP picked producers that were not stunning, and very few shrimp producers anywhere bought stunners before the program; several partners are linked to UK and EU buyers (Labeyrie, Young's/Sofina, Tesco) that are moving towards stunning, which is the low end's 60%.

rows.label: Shrimp Welfare Project's share of credit
rows.explainer: SWP pays for the stunner and the technical support; producers pay freight, import duties, installation, electricity and staff time, so they share the cost of the outcome. Retailer and importer stunning policies are not counted here: whether they would have led to stunning anyway is in counterfactual_adj and years_of_impact. Best guess 90% to SWP, its rough share of the cost of getting a stunner running; low 75% if producers' installation and running costs are larger than we think; high 100%. Switch on full credit to give SWP all of it.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment: stunners installed and used on the committed volume
rows.explainer: The share of the committed shrimp that actually pass through a working stunner. The stunners counted here are ones SWP has bought, not agreements: the accounts show about 12 bought by March 2025 and SWP reports 20 installed and commissioned by autumn 2026, so stunners bought in the year are very likely installed (the delay of up to a year is not discounted separately and costs about 4%). What remains uncertain is use: SWP says its shrimp numbers are 'a projection based on signed commitments — not a count of shrimp that have already been stunned', and its monitoring of verified use is still being built. Shortfalls come from stunners used on only part of a producer's harvest (for example away from the processing plant), downtime and agreements that lapse (SWP can reclaim stunners, which limits this). Best guess 80%; low 60% if partial use is common; high 95% if installed stunners run on the whole committed volume.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above: about 0.43 at the best guesses.

rows.label: SADs averted
rows.explainer: Shrimp stunned per year × discounted years brought forward × SADs averted per shrimp × adjustments.

rows.label: SADs averted per dollar

rows.explainer: Almost all of SWP's team worked as contractors in the year (one employee on average). They work like staff, so they count towards the staff cost share. It includes the co-founders' service fees disclosed in note 7.

source.quote: Salaries and wages 40,159 Social security costs 4,205 44,364

rows.explainer: Payroll for the one employee the charity had on average in the year.

rows.label: Staff and contractor pay as a share of total cost
rows.explainer: People costs (contractors plus payroll) over total cash spending, about 43%, organisation-wide. The stunner program's own people share is lower (about 30–35%) because stunners are about two thirds of its cost; using the organisation-wide share understates the result by about 4%.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable for-profit jobs
rows.explainer: How much less SWP's team earns than in comparable roles elsewhere. The repo's reference class is about 15% for large delivery charities and 35% for advocacy groups. SWP is in between: field coordinators in Vietnam, India and Latin America are paid local rates for aquaculture technical work, while the leadership (with consulting, research and corporate backgrounds) likely earns well below what it could. Best guess 25%, range 10–40%.
